checks.claim: Harvey measured how much blood the heart holds and reckoned its beats: left ventricle holds upwards of two ounces (in a dead body); more than a thousand beats in half an hour; so in half an hour more blood is sent out than the whole body contains (De Motu Cordis, ch. 9)
checks.note: He estimated the beat count rather than counting it in one sitting, but 'counted how often it beats' is a fair child-level gloss.

checks.claim: Book of 1628 (De Motu Cordis, Frankfurt); Harvey an English physician

Wrong: the liver makes new blood from food very quickly (Galen's model; Harvey showed no food intake could supply such a quantity)
Wrong: the flesh uses up blood as fast as it comes (Galen's consumption idea, overturned by the reckoning)
Wrong: the heart makes new blood with every beat; context 'the heart makes no blood at all; it only pumps it'
Context: Galen, a Greek doctor of Roman times, taught the liver makes blood from food and the body uses it up; followed for centuries
checks.note: Galen of Pergamon, 129-c.216 CE; his physiology shaped medicine for over a millennium.

checks.claim: Harvey's band (ligature) on a living man's arm: veins below it swell, knots show where the valves are
checks.note: Harvey: 'let anyone make an experiment upon the arm of a man'; the knots 'are all formed by valves'.

checks.claim: Key: blood can be pushed only up the arm, toward the heart (pushing toward the hand, 'you cannot force the blood through or beyond the valve'; streaked upward, the vein refills only from below)
Wrong choices (only down; both ways; neither way) are wrong
Context: Galen taught the veins carry blood out from the liver to the limbs
Context: 'The valves had been found by his teacher, Hieronymus Fabricius'
checks.note: Fabricius (Harvey's teacher at Padua) gave the first detailed description and drawings (De venarum ostiolis, 1603), and Grokipedia credits him with the observation, but Linda Hall says 'the valves had been noticed several times before', and the history literature names Charles Estienne (1545), Canano (1547, reported by Amatus Lusitanus) and Sylvius earlier. Harvey himself notes Riolan credited Sylvius. Fix: 'The valves had been described and drawn by his teacher, Hieronymus Fabricius, but it was Harvey who showed what they are for.' (Fabricius thought they kept blood from pooling in the hands and feet.)

Marcello Malpighi, an Italian doctor (physician; MD Bologna 1653)

Context: an organ is built of several kinds of tissue; cells form tissues, tissues organs, organs organ systems, systems the organism

Context: blood turned away from gut and kidneys by up to three-quarters; vessels in working muscle widen
Context: HER heart raises its output 'from about 5 litres of blood a minute at rest to 20 litres or more'
checks.note: Grokipedia gives 5 L/min at rest rising to 20-25 L/min for untrained or moderately trained ADULTS. Measured peaks for women are lower (young women about 17.7 L/min, PMC2838638; a 500-person reference study averaged 11.0 L/min for women, pubmed 28108178), and a schoolgirl, being smaller, rests below 5 and peaks well under 20 (adolescent girls' maximal cardiac index about 7 L/min per square metre). As written, the adult-male figure is pinned on 'her'. Fix: 'Her heart beats faster and harder, pumping three or four times as much blood each minute as at rest (a grown man goes from about 5 litres a minute to 20 or more), while...'

unit_notes: Tone is clinical throughout (emphysema, diarrhoea, kidney failure 'untreated, can kill' are all plain and factual). Harvey's ch. 9 reckoning and arm-valve demonstration are told as Harvey wrote them (Fordham sourcebook text). Two soft spots: (1) 7c1df58cf6 credits Fabricius with having 'found' the vein valves; he described and drew them (1603), but others had noticed them earlier: say 'described'. (2) 4441bd3c2d gives an adult's 5 to 20+ L/min cardiac-output figure as the sprinting girl's own; restate as a multiple or attribute the litres to an adult. Optional: 2d736ef41d's 'Dialysis runs the blood through a filter outside the body' is true of haemodialysis, the commonest kind, not of peritoneal dialysis.
